subject: log size transformation in allometry tests - necessary?

messages.author: 8bcb7cabc778c7da
messages.subject: log size transformation in allometry tests - necessary?
parts:
Dear all,

I'm embarrassed to ask this question, so please forgive me if it's too simple.

I'm wondering what is the significance of log-transforming size in allometry tests, for example using procD.lm and procD.allometry.

For all of these tests I have multiple groups (species), and they have significantly different ontogenetic allometries. So far I have been running all tests using a skull length measurement instead of centroid size, because it's easier to directly relate the points in the output graphs to specimens in my sample, which is important for describing when during growth certain changes occur, e.g., after weaning or tooth eruption.

Log-transforming size doesn't change the results much, but it does change the graphical outputs, for example when plotting CAC on skull length vs log-skull length. I understand the value of log transformation in linear regression and to visualize equal units of change along the x-axis, but I'm not sure it's necessary for these types of tests. My skull lengths range from ~8-242 mm.

Thanks for any advice on this,
Christy

messages.author: 511e44c7d1e1bab0
messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] log size transformation in allometry tests - necessary?
parts:
Hi Christy,

I don't think this question is basic or simple at all, actually it is a very good one!

Generally, log-transformation will bring your data closer to normality, and also make variation relative to the scale of the trait, which (at least for me) helps interpretation, especially when looking at different groups, which might have different ranges and variances. But I am not surprised your results do not change much with and without logs for CS (or, put another way, if that where the case I would tend to think more about statistical or sample artifacts, rather than a biologically interpretable pattern).

Hope this helps

Antigoni

messages.author: aab55242ff4da6c6
messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] log size transformation in allometry tests - necessary?
parts:
One could also argue that there is a biological reasoning rather than a statistical one.  Many morphological and physiological attribute scale exponentially with size (e.g., mass and metabolic rate), especially if such attributes tend to correspond more so with volume or surface area, rather than linear distance (as how size was classically measured). I have often wondered if centroid size, although univariate, behaves more like a volume than a linear distance with its correlation of shape. One could probably confirm this with simulations - I have not bothered.  Anyway, because log transformation converts an exponential relationship to a linear one - which is helpful for least-squares based statistics - the biological and statistical reasons for doing it are in concert. However, I think doing this with centroid size is a relic from days when size was measured as a linear distance, and because it does not impose a problem (I think) it just sort of sticks around as convention. 

A good policy is to address the distribution of residuals and use a transformation (or not) based on the their best “behavior” (tending toward multivariate normality and homoscedasticty). 

Mike

messages.author: 8bcb7cabc778c7da
messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] log size transformation in allometry tests - necessary?
parts:
Thanks for your answers. So it sounds like it's not necessarily wrong to use the true size value in allometry tests, but that log-transforming can make interpretation easier. 

Regarding normality, I looked at both the size and log-size variables and neither are normally distributed (this is for the entire dataset, not within species). I also checked the residuals from a regression of shape on size, and those are (at least checking several of them separately, although I didn't do this in a multivariate sense). When I run the allometry tests with and without log-transforming, the R2 is slightly higher for true size but the F and Z values are slightly lower. Again, none of this actually changes the overall interpretation of the results so I feel it's more an aesthetic issue at this point regarding graphics. I do see how log-size on the x-axis makes it easier to see species differences (mine range from mouse-size to wolf-size), but it just means I have to backtrack to the true value to get to the actual specimen and developmental stage.

I don't mean to beleaguer the point, but as Mike points out, it seems to be a standard regarding centroid size so I wasn't sure about other (linear) variables.

I'm happy for any more input, and thanks again for your feedback.

Christy

messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] log size transformation in allometry tests - necessary?
parts:
Christy,

The normality assumption is for residuals, not the covariate, size.  If you use plot.procD.lm, you can generate diagnostic plots to check some of the important assumptions, much like plot.lm for univariate data.

Mike
